title: Mobile latency sink sweep — personal scratch
content:
Context:
Quick personal sweep to understand how simulated mobile RTT (50ms-300ms) interacts with our streaming path and client-side sinks. Goal is to capture qualitative and quantitative differences between streaming vs non-streaming payload shapes and to surface small performance tuning ideas (chunk sizing, flush frequency, client backpressure).

Test matrix (high level):
- Model: small-1.3B-ish demo build (dense, KV cache enabled)
- Hosts: single GPU dev node (A100) with local redis mimic, no autoscaling
- Workload shapes: short prompts (~40 tokens) and long prompts (~600 tokens), mostly single-turn generation to isolate output streaming behavior
- Client RTT simulated at network layer: 50ms (good 4G), 120ms (typical 4G uplink), 250-300ms (poor mobile/edge)
- Modes: streaming (chunk-size heuristic = 64 tokens / 150ms flush), non-streaming (batch return after model finishes), chunked-early (flush every 32 tokens), client-sink-pressure (client sends ACKs on receipt to throttle)
- Concurrency: 1, 4, 16 concurrent clients
- Metric focus: p50/p90/p99 server-side tail, user-perceived completion time (first-chunk time, final-complete), tokens/sec, effective throughput (tokens/sec per GPU)

Raw observations (notes-to-self):
- Streaming buys perceived speed: first-chunk time consistently ~model-init + RTT. At 50ms RTT, perceived early response < 150ms for short prompts. At 250ms RTT, first-chunk delayed by ~200-250ms as expected, but still earlier than wait-for-complete in many cases (user sees something earlier).
- Non-streaming completion time often wins at high RTT for short outputs: when total generation is <~300ms, the extra RTTs from repeated small TCP frames for streaming can push perceived-first-chunk later than the monolithic return. i.e., streaming hurts if model can produce quickly and network latency is high.
- Chunked-early (every 32 tokens) reduces perceived-first-chunk slightly vs 64-token flush, but increases total requests/frames and marginally raises server CPU and kernel scheduling overhead. Need to measure CPU climb at high concurrency.
- Client ACK-driven sink is useful: when client pauses reads (simulated by delaying ACKs), our runtime stalls KV-cache warmup for that stream and other multiplexed requests on same connection show tail jitter. This is a notable head-of-line sensitivity for multiplexed worker models.

Selected numeric run (short prompt, token budget ~40):
Mode | RTT | concurrency | first-chunk p50 | final-complete p50 | p99 final (ms)
streaming (64/150ms) | 50ms | 4 | 110ms | 240ms | 540ms
streaming (64/150ms) | 250ms | 4 | 320ms | 520ms | 1100ms
non-streaming | 50ms | 4 | 210ms | 210ms | 480ms
non-streaming | 250ms | 4 | 470ms | 470ms | 980ms
chunked (32 tokens) | 120ms | 4 | 200ms | 410ms | 720ms

Interpretation of numbers above (quick):
- At 50ms RTT streaming gives very snappy first-chunk; end-to-end also often faster because network overhead small compared to generation.
- At 250ms RTT streaming first-chunk still earlier than non-streaming, but the overhead stacks for multi-chunk cases so final-complete can be worse. For single-chunk short outputs, non-streaming equals or beats streaming.
- p99 tails are dominated by two factors: CPU scheduling spikes on host during small-chunk flushes, and client-side ACK delays causing internal stall.

Micro-profiling notes (observed from dev VM):
- Increased syscalls with chunked-early: +23% write syscalls/sec under 16 concurrency.
- Kernel wakeups correlated with flush timer (150ms) spikes: when flush timer is 150ms we see more wakeups grouped at flush boundaries -> CPU hot-pockets -> jitter.
- KV-cache hits unaffected by streaming mode for these experiments; however cache priming (first generation after idle) tends to be most impacted by client-side pause on sink.

Quick heuristics to test further (TODO actionable experiments):
1) Adaptive flush: switch flush timer based on current RTT estimate (if RTT > 180ms, prefer larger chunk flush or single return for short output).
2) Combine streaming with final-burst coalescing: stream first chunk early, but then if subsequent chunks are small and RTT large, coalesce last chunks into single final payload to reduce frame count.
3) Client-side guidance header: let client send preferred mode hint (fast-first, low-bandwidth) so server can choose chunking. Add X-Client-Mode in request metadata for experiment.
4) Backpressure-sensitivity isolation: move streaming per-connection sink to per-stream queue to avoid head-of-line stalls across multiplexed streams (cost: more memory).
5) Expose a per-route flush_tuning suggestion in Console Optimize page (approx algorithm notes).

Hypotheses to validate (pri order):
- H1: Adaptive flush timer tuned to RTT reduces p99 for streaming at high RTT without impacting p50 at low RTT.
- H2: Client ACK delays (simulated bad client) create disproportionate tail amplification for multiplexed sessions compared to one-connection-per-stream.
- H3: Chunk-size tradeoff has non-linear CPU overhead that matters above ~8 concurrency (test with 8,16,32).

Notes on experiment artifacts and next steps:
- Need scripted harness: use wrk-like harness to simulate per-connection RTT + programmable client read pauses. Right now used ad-hoc netem and custom python streamer client. Put this in a small repo CI job.
- Capture tcpdump + strace on a couple of runs to correlate syscall bursts with kernel wakeups.
- Run same sweep against Dedicated config (pinned GPU) to see differences when autoscaler not present. Also run with small quantized model to see CPU differences.
- Share initial findings with Talia and SRE: ask for ideas on kernel wakeup mitigation and for advice on safe per-stream queues.

Checklist and quick TODOs (short):
- [ ] Build harness (wrk variant) + add RTT profiles (50/120/250/350ms)
- [ ] Add adaptive-flush prototype (server-side toggle) behind feature flag
- [ ] Run concurrency scaling (1,4,8,16,32) for chunking strategies
- [ ] Collect strace/tcpdump during high-p99 runs
- [ ] Draft short one-pager for product: "Streaming heuristics for mobile" with recs

Open questions / fuzzy bits:
- How will this interact with function/tool-calls where outputs can be very bursty? (likely similar; tool-call latency amplification could be worse)
- Are there meaningful differences between HTTP/1.1 chunked vs HTTP/2 flow control for our runtime? Need to replicate tests with both transport modes.
- If we move to per-stream in-memory sinks we add memory pressure—what's the safe per-tenant bound? (need SRE input)

One-line summary to keep: "Streaming improves perceived latency on mobile when RTT is moderate, but naive small-chunk flushing at high RTT increases tail and CPU wakeups; adaptive flush strategies can give the best of both worlds."

Scratch log (timestamps):
- 2024-10-11 10:32: initial ad-hoc sweep, noticed p99 jump on chunked flows
- 2024-10-14 15:09: verified that client read pausing amplifies tail across multiplexed streams
- 2024-11-02 09:17: measured syscall delta with chunk-size change
- 2025-02-05 16:42: re-ran short prompt matrix, wrote this summary and TODOs

Random notes-to-self: keep the harness deterministic (seeded RNG for jitter), and add explicit accounting for TLS handshake costs (mobile often re-uses connections but some clients don't).

End of scratch.
